Introduction to AWS Command Line Interface and EC2 Connection Options

Learn the structure of an AWS CLI command, how the CLI uses IAM, profiles, and Regions, how to automate with scripts, and how to connect to EC2 and use AWS CloudShell.

Overview and Objectives

Lesson Overview

In this lesson, you explore how to interact with AWS and manage resources efficiently by using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). The AWS Management Console provides a graphical interface. The AWS CLI offers speed and simplicity, which makes it a preferred choice for engineers and power users. You also compare the ways to connect to an Amazon EC2 instance, and you use AWS CloudShell.

This lesson matters for the AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate (SAA-C03) exam. The exam tests that the CLI is a fast and scriptable alternative to the console, that the CLI does not bypass IAM permissions, and that IAM roles and temporary credentials are preferred over hard-coded access keys. It also tests configuration details, such as the difference between aws configure and aws configure sso, and troubleshooting with the --region and --profile flags and with aws sts get-caller-identity. Scripts that use the AWS CLI improve consistency and reduce manual errors.

This lesson supports the Module 267 scenario, in which you help RetailCloud. The last tab checks what you learned.

The tabs in this lesson cover the following topics:

  • Tab 1: what the AWS CLI is, the structure of a command, parameter values, installation, the built-in help, and basic EC2 examples.
  • Tab 2: how the CLI uses IAM permissions, profiles, and Regions, the exam tips, an example automation scenario, and a simple script.
  • Tab 3: the ways to connect to an EC2 instance, EC2 Instance Connect, AWS CloudShell, and the two hands-on labs.
  • Tab 4: open-ended Knowledge Check questions with model answers.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, learners will be able to:

  1. Identify the core components of an AWS CLI command structure, including base commands, subcommands, options, and parameters.
  2. Explain how the AWS CLI integrates with IAM permissions, authentication profiles, and regional settings.
  3. Execute AWS CLI commands to perform common resource management operations, such as inspecting and controlling EC2 instances and S3 buckets.
  4. Analyze operational scenarios to select appropriate AWS CLI flags.
  5. Construct shell scripts using the AWS CLI to automate routine cloud infrastructure management tasks while adhering to security best practices.

1. AWS CLI Basics

Problem Statement

RetailCloud’s developers click through the AWS Management Console to look up instances and to stop development servers. The work is slow, and each person does it a little differently. The operations lead wants a faster, repeatable method.

The architect introduces the AWS CLI and shows how a command is built, how to install it, and how to find help.

Your challenge:

  • Name the parts of an AWS CLI command.
  • Install the AWS CLI and use its built-in help.
  • Run basic EC2 commands, and select a Region for a command.

1.1 What Is the AWS CLI?

The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) is an open-source tool that lets you interact with AWS services by using commands in your command-line shell. It provides functionality equivalent to the browser-based AWS Management Console, from the command prompt in your terminal program:

  • Linux shells: use common shell programs such as bash, zsh, and tcsh to run commands in Linux or macOS.
  • Windows command line: on Windows, run commands at the Windows command prompt or in PowerShell.

1.2 Command Structure

The AWS CLI uses a multipart structure on the command line. You must specify the parts in this order:

  1. The base call to the aws program.
  2. The top-level command, which typically corresponds to an AWS service that the AWS CLI supports.
  3. The subcommand, which specifies which operation to perform.
  4. General AWS CLI options or parameters that the operation requires. You can specify these in any order as long as they follow the first three parts. If you specify an exclusive parameter more than once, only the last value applies.
aws <command> <subcommand> [options and parameters]

Parameters can take various types of input values, such as numbers, strings, lists, maps, and JSON structures. What is supported depends on the command and the subcommand that you specify.

1.2.1 Example CLI Command: Amazon S3

The following example lists all of your Amazon S3 buckets:

aws s3 ls

Expected result (the bucket names and dates are examples):

2026-09-11 17:08:50 amzn-s3-demo-bucket1
2026-09-14 14:55:44 amzn-s3-demo-bucket2

The command means:

  • aws: run the AWS CLI.
  • s3: use Amazon S3.
  • ls: list the available S3 buckets and objects.

1.3 Specifying Parameter Values

Many parameters in the AWS CLI are simple string or numeric values, such as the key pair name my-key-pair in the following aws ec2 create-key-pair command:

aws ec2 create-key-pair --key-name my-key-pair

1.4 Installing the Latest Version of the AWS CLI

Before you use the AWS CLI, you must install it. Visit the official AWS website to install the latest version of the AWS CLI.

Mandatory Video

Watch the video How to Install AWS CLI in Windows (Full Guide) on YouTube before the first lab. If it does not play in this page, open the link in a new tab.

1.5 The Built-In AWS CLI Help Command

The AWS CLI has built-in help. When you add help to a command, you see detailed documentation, including descriptions, synopses, and the available global options. To open the help for the AWS CLI, run:

aws help

The following command displays the Amazon EC2 specific commands:

aws ec2 help

The following command displays detailed help for the Amazon EC2 DescribeInstances operation. The help includes descriptions of its input parameters, the available filters, and what the output contains. It also includes examples that show how to type common variations of the command.

aws ec2 describe-instances help

1.6 Examples

1.6.1 List EC2 Instances

aws ec2 describe-instances

1.6.2 Start an EC2 Instance

aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids i-0123456789abcdef0

1.6.3 Stop an EC2 Instance

aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-0123456789abcdef0

1.6.4 Specify a Region

aws ec2 describe-instances --region us-west-2

2. Credentials, Regions, and Automation

Problem Statement

RetailCloud’s nightly stop script runs on an EC2 instance. The security team asks how the script gets its permissions, whether access keys are stored in it, which account the commands run in, and how the team targets the production account safely.

The architect explains how the AWS CLI relates to IAM and shows an automation that follows the security practices.

Your challenge:

  • Explain how the AWS CLI relates to IAM permissions, profiles, and Regions.
  • Choose the right flag for a multi-account or multi-Region scenario.
  • Describe a safe, repeatable automation with the AWS CLI.

2.1 Exam Tips: Identity, Profiles, and Regions

  • The AWS CLI can perform many of the same operations that are available through the AWS Management Console.
  • The CLI does not bypass IAM permissions.
  • Prefer IAM roles and temporary credentials over hard-coded access keys.
  • An EC2 instance should use an instance role when it runs AWS CLI commands.
  • aws configure creates a local CLI configuration. It does not create an IAM user.
  • aws configure sso configures CLI access through IAM Identity Center.
  • Use --region to select a Region for a command.
  • Use --profile when you work with multiple accounts or configurations.
  • Use aws sts get-caller-identity to confirm which identity and account the CLI is using.
  • Scripts that use the AWS CLI can improve consistency and reduce manual administration.

For example, the following command lists the instances in the account and Region that the dev profile selects, and the second command shows the identity that the profile uses:

aws ec2 describe-instances --profile dev --region us-west-2
aws sts get-caller-identity --profile dev

Memory aid: the AWS Management Console is graphical, while the AWS CLI manages AWS resources by using commands and scripts.

2.2 Example Scenario: Managing EC2 Instances

2.2.1 Business Situation

A company runs development EC2 instances only during business hours. Developers often forget to stop the instances overnight, which creates unnecessary cost.

2.2.2 AWS CLI Solution

A scheduled automation runs the following command at the end of the workday:

aws ec2 stop-instances \
  --instance-ids i-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --region us-east-1

The instance can be started the next morning:

aws ec2 start-instances \
  --instance-ids i-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --region us-east-1

In a larger environment, the automation could identify development instances by tags, instead of keeping a manually written list of instance IDs.

2.3 A Simple Script With Tags

This illustrative script puts the idea of tags into practice. It finds the running instances that have the tag Environment=dev and stops them. Replace the tag with one of your own, and test the script in a non-production account first.

#!/bin/bash
# Stop the running instances that have the tag Environment=dev.
REGION=us-east-1

IDS=$(aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --region "$REGION" \
  --filters "Name=tag:Environment,Values=dev" "Name=instance-state-name,Values=running" \
  --query "Reservations[].Instances[].InstanceId" \
  --output text)

if [ -n "$IDS" ]; then
  aws ec2 stop-instances --region "$REGION" --instance-ids $IDS
fi
  • No access keys in the script. When the script runs on an EC2 instance, the instance role supplies temporary credentials, and the role should allow only the actions that the script needs.
  • The Region is explicit. The --region option selects the Region for each command.
  • Tags replace a hand-written list. The filters select the instances, so the script keeps working when instances change.

3. Connecting to EC2 and AWS CloudShell

Problem Statement

RetailCloud’s administrators must reach Linux and Windows instances without exposing them to the whole internet. They also sometimes need a quick CLI session without installing tools on a laptop.

The architect compares the connection methods and introduces AWS CloudShell.

Your challenge:

  • Choose a connection method for a stated situation.
  • Describe EC2 Instance Connect.
  • Explain what AWS CloudShell is, and name its limits.

3.1 Ways to Interact With an Amazon EC2 Instance

Lesson 267.3 introduces these methods. The table repeats them for this lesson.

#Connection methodOperating systemDescription
1SSH clientLinuxConnect with an SSH client such as OpenSSH, Terminal, PowerShell, or PuTTY. The instance must be reachable over the network, and its security group normally allows inbound TCP port 22 from an approved IP address.
2Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) clientWindowsConnect with Microsoft Remote Desktop or another RDP client. The instance must be reachable, and its security group normally allows inbound TCP port 3389 from an approved IP address.
3EC2 Instance ConnectLinuxConnect through the EC2 console, the AWS CLI, or an SSH client. EC2 Instance Connect sends a temporary SSH public key to the instance. The instance must have EC2 Instance Connect installed and allow SSH traffic on port 22.
4AWS Systems Manager Session ManagerLinux and WindowsStart a secure command-line session from the AWS console or the AWS CLI. The instance does not need a public IP address or an inbound SSH or RDP rule. The instance must be managed by Systems Manager and have the required IAM permissions and SSM Agent.
5EC2 Instance Connect EndpointLinux and WindowsCreates a secure tunnel to an instance through its private IP address. The instance does not need a public IP address, an internet gateway, a VPN, or a bastion host. It supports SSH for Linux and RDP for Windows. Appropriate IAM permissions and security group rules are required.
6Systems Manager Fleet Manager Remote DesktopWindowsProvides browser-based Remote Desktop access to a Windows instance. It uses Systems Manager, so you can manage the instance without exposing RDP port 3389 directly to the internet.
7AWS CloudShellPrimarily Linux, through SSH or the AWS CLICloudShell provides a browser-based, preauthenticated command-line environment. You can use it to run AWS CLI commands or start an SSH connection, but CloudShell is not itself an EC2 remote-access service. The EC2 instance must still be reachable through an appropriate network path.

Connecting from Windows: you can connect with the built-in OpenSSH client in Windows Terminal, PowerShell, or Command Prompt. If OpenSSH is unavailable, or you prefer a graphical SSH client, you can install PuTTY at no cost from the official PuTTY download page.

3.1.1 Which Option Works From Which Computer

The table shows which ways of connecting you can use from each type of computer. EC2 Instance Connect runs in a browser from the console, so it works from any of them. The instance must still allow the connection, as the table above describes.

Your computerSSH clientPuTTYEC2 Instance Connect
MacYes (built in)Not neededYes (in a browser)
LinuxYes (built in)Not neededYes (in a browser)
Windows 10 and laterYes (built-in OpenSSH client)Yes (free download)Yes (in a browser)

Rebuilt from the SSH summary table in the course lesson document, and updated for current versions of Windows.

3.2 EC2 Instance Connect

  • EC2 Instance Connect sends a temporary SSH public key to the instance, so you do not manage a long-lived key file for the connection.
  • You can connect through the EC2 console, the AWS CLI, or an SSH client. The instance must have EC2 Instance Connect installed and allow SSH traffic on port 22.
  • EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint reaches an instance through its private IP address, with no public IP address, internet gateway, VPN, or bastion host.

The animation shows the console steps: open EC2 from Console Home, select the instance, choose Connect, and keep the default username on the EC2 Instance Connect tab. AWS keeps a current comparison of all the methods in the official EC2 connection guide.

3.3 AWS CloudShell

  • AWS CloudShell runs CLI commands directly in the browser.
  • It lets you run AWS CLI commands without installing or configuring command-line tools on your local computer.

CloudShell is useful for:

  • Running AWS CLI commands from a web browser.
  • Testing commands before you add them to scripts.
  • Uploading and downloading files.
  • Using preinstalled command-line tools.
  • Avoiding a local AWS CLI installation and configuration.

3.3.1 Preinstalled Tools on CloudShell

CloudShell includes commonly used tools such as the AWS CLI, Bash, Python, Git, text editors, and file-transfer utilities.

3.3.2 Region Awareness

Note: CloudShell is not available in all Regions. Check the list in Supported AWS Regions for AWS CloudShell, because AWS adds Regions over time.

CloudShell operates in a supported AWS Region. Commands normally use the Region that is associated with the CloudShell session, unless you specify another Region. To check the current Region, run:

aws configure get region

To specify a different Region for a command, run:

aws ec2 describe-instances --region us-west-2

3.3.3 How to Start and Access CloudShell

Select the CloudShell icon on the console toolbar, or choose CloudShell at the lower left of the console.

The next screenshot marks the key features of the CloudShell interface:

  1. AWS CloudShell is a command-line interface in which you run commands by using your preferred shell. The command prompt shows the current shell type.
  2. The terminal tab (for example, us-east-1) shows the AWS Region where CloudShell is currently running.
  3. The + icon opens a menu with options to create, restart, and delete environments.
  4. The Actions menu has options for changing the screen layout, downloading and uploading files, restarting your CloudShell, and deleting your CloudShell home directory. The Download option is not available when you launch CloudShell from the console toolbar.
  5. Open in a new browser tab gives you the option to use your CloudShell session in full screen.
  6. Preferences lets you customize your shell experience.
  7. The bottom bar lets you launch CloudShell from the CloudShell icon and send feedback from the Feedback icon. To send feedback, choose the type of feedback, add your comments, and then choose Submit.

3.3.4 Important Limitations

  • CloudShell is designed primarily for administration and development tasks.
  • It is not intended to host production applications.
  • Sessions have resource and duration limits.
  • Do not treat files as permanent backups.
  • Your actions are limited by your IAM permissions.
  • Some network access patterns may need additional configuration or a different service.

3.6 Lesson Summary

In this lesson, you learned the following:

  • The AWS CLI is an open-source tool for managing AWS services with commands in a shell, and it does not bypass AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions.
  • An AWS CLI command follows this order: the base call to aws, the top-level command, the subcommand, and then the options and parameters.
  • The built-in help command, such as aws ec2 help, displays the available commands and the details of each operation.
  • The --region option selects the Region for a single command, and the --profile option selects a configuration when you work with more than one account or configuration.
  • The aws configure command creates a local configuration, the aws configure sso command sets up access through IAM Identity Center, and the aws sts get-caller-identity command confirms the identity and account in use.
  • IAM roles and temporary credentials are preferred over hard-coded access keys, and an Amazon EC2 instance should use an instance role when it runs AWS CLI commands.
  • You can connect to an Amazon EC2 instance with an SSH client, an RDP client, EC2 Instance Connect, Session Manager, EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint, or Systems Manager Fleet Manager Remote Desktop.
  • Session Manager does not need a public IP address or an inbound SSH or RDP rule.
  • AWS CloudShell is a browser-based environment for running AWS CLI commands without a local installation, and it is intended for administration and development tasks, not for hosting production applications.

4. Knowledge Check

Answer each question in your own words before you open the model answer. The questions were written for this course.

Question 1: Break down the command aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 into its parts, and say what each part does.

Maps to: Objective 1 (Comprehension).

The word aws is the base call that runs the AWS CLI program. The word ec2 is the top-level command, which names the service. The word stop-instances is the subcommand, the operation to perform. The options --instance-ids and --region, with their values, are the options and parameters. They name the instance to stop and the Region for the command, and they follow the first three parts.

Question 2: How does the AWS CLI interact with IAM permissions? What is the difference between aws configure and aws configure sso?

Maps to: Objective 2 (Comprehension).

The CLI does not bypass IAM permissions. Every command runs as an identity, and AWS allows it only if that identity has the permission. The command aws configure creates a local CLI configuration, and it does not create an IAM user. The command aws configure sso sets up CLI access through IAM Identity Center. IAM roles and temporary credentials are preferred over hard-coded access keys.

Question 3: A team works in two AWS accounts and two Regions. Which flags target each, and which command confirms the identity in use?

Maps to: Objective 4 (Application).

Use --profile to select the configuration for an account, and use --region to select the Region for a command. To confirm which identity and account the CLI is using, run aws sts get-caller-identity.

Question 4: Which commands list, start, and stop EC2 instances? How do you find the options for the DescribeInstances operation?

Maps to: Objective 3 (Application).

Use aws ec2 describe-instances to list instances, aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids to start them, and aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids to stop them. To see the parameters, filters, and output for DescribeInstances, run aws ec2 describe-instances help.

Question 5: A script on an EC2 instance stops the development instances every night. How should it get its permissions, and how can it find the instances without a hard-coded list?

Maps to: Objective 5 (Synthesis).

Assign an instance role, so that the script uses temporary credentials and stores no access keys, and give the role only the permissions the script needs. Use tags to find the instances, for example with a filter on a tag such as Environment=dev and on the running state, and select the Region explicitly with --region.

Question 6: An EC2 instance has no public IP address and no inbound SSH or RDP rule. How can an administrator open a command-line session, and what must be true of the instance?

Maps to: Lesson goal: connection options (Application).

Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager. The instance must be managed by Systems Manager and have the required IAM permissions and the SSM Agent. If the administrator needs SSH or RDP through a private IP address, EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint is another option.

Question 7: Which connection method gives a browser-based desktop for a Windows instance, and which method reaches an instance through its private IP address with no bastion host?

Maps to: Lesson goal: connection options (Comprehension).

Systems Manager Fleet Manager Remote Desktop gives browser-based Remote Desktop access to a Windows instance without exposing port 3389 to the internet. EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint creates a secure tunnel through the private IP address, with no public IP address, internet gateway, VPN, or bastion host.

Question 8: What is AWS CloudShell, what is it useful for, and what are its limits?

Maps to: Lesson goal: AWS CloudShell (Comprehension).

CloudShell is a browser-based, preauthenticated command-line environment that runs AWS CLI commands without a local installation. It is useful for running and testing commands, uploading and downloading files, and using the preinstalled tools. It is designed for administration and development tasks. It is not intended to host production applications, sessions have resource and duration limits, files are not permanent backups, and your actions are limited by your IAM permissions.
